[PATH:empirical] A randomized controlled trial comparing intermittent fasting with protein-pacing (IF-P) to daily caloric restriction (DCR) over 12-24 months in adults without metabolic disorders, with weight loss and body composition as primary outcomes. — Direct head-to-head long-term RCT is the gold standard to test the hypothesis that IF-P is more effective than DCR for sustained weight loss, controlling for adherence and dietary composition.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of post-2010 Western studies on IF-P versus DCR for weight maintenance beyond 12 months, including subgroup analysis for metabolic health status. — Synthesizing existing evidence can reveal patterns of effect size, heterogeneity, and moderators (e.g., protein timing, pacing schedule) that support or refute the superiority claim, especially given the disputed status.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal cohort study examining adherence and metabolic adaptations (e.g., resting metabolic rate, hormonal changes) in adults practicing IF-P versus DCR over 12+ months, with weight regain as a secondary endpoint. — Understanding mechanisms such as metabolic compensation or appetite regulation can explain why IF-P might or might not outperform DCR in the long term, informing causal inference beyond simple weight outcomes.

[PATH:empirical] Long-term prospective cohort study (≥12 months) in adults without metabolic disorders, using objective adherence measures (e.g., continuous glucose monitors or digital food logs) for both daily restriction and intermittent fasting groups — High-quality empirical data with objective adherence tracking can reduce self-report bias and clarify whether observed effects hold beyond short-term trials, especially for sustained weight loss.

[PATH:theoretical] Mathematical modeling of energy balance and adaptive thermogenesis under daily restriction vs. intermittent fasting protocols, incorporating hormonal and metabolic adaptation data — Theoretical models can predict long-term weight loss trajectories based on known physiological mechanisms (e.g., ghrelin, leptin, insulin), helping to identify whether any differential effects are plausible over 12+ months.
